relations.note: Jupiter assumes Amphitryon’s appearance and becomes Hercules’ biological divine father.

relations.myth: Apotheosis after the pyre on Oeta
relations.note: Jupiter preserves Hercules’ divine part and receives him into heaven.
Alcmena is Hercules’ mortal mother in the dominant Greek-Roman genealogy.
Amphitryon is Hercules’ social father, though Jupiter is his biological father.
Iphicles is Hercules’ mortal twin or half-brother.

relations.myth: Juno persecutes the infant and sends serpents
relations.note: Juno’s hostility begins in infancy when she sends serpents against Hercules.

relations.myth: Juno drives Hercules into murderous madness
relations.note: Juno inflicts madness that makes Hercules kill his family.
After prolonged hostility, Juno reluctantly accepts Hercules into divine order.

relations.myth: Uni adopts or reconciles with Hercle
relations.note: An Etruscan mirror calls Hercle “son of Uni,” presenting divine adoption.
Hebe becomes Hercules’ divine wife after his ascent to heaven.

relations.myth: Minerva repeatedly assists and receives Hercules
relations.note: Minerva helps Hercules and receives him into divine order.
Etruscan images pair Mercury with Hercules as a mediator of divine presentation.
Hercules struggles with Apollo after being refused purification or an oracle.

relations.myth: Capture of the sacred Ceryneian hind
relations.note: Hercules captures Diana’s hind without killing it and explains his task.
Hercules wounds Ares while defending Pylos.
Hercules sacks Troy after Neptune and Apollo had built its walls.
Some versions have Hercules wound Hades during his underworld descent.
Hercules encounters Proserpina while attempting to rescue Theseus and Pirithous.

relations.myth: Rescue of Theseus from the underworld
relations.note: Hercules frees Theseus during his descent for Cerberus.
Hercules attempts but in some accounts cannot rescue Pirithous.
Hercules defeats the transforming river-god and breaks off one horn.
Hercules tricks Atlas into resuming the sky after obtaining the apples.

relations.myth: Hercules becomes leader and guardian of the Muses
relations.note: Hercules is presented as the Muses’ companion, guardian, or leader.

relations.myth: Exclusion from Bona Dea’s women-only sanctuary
relations.note: Denied water, Hercules forces entry and retaliates by excluding women from his altar.
Carmenta recognizes Jupiter’s son and prophesies his future apotheosis.

relations.myth: Reform of Saturnian practices in Italy
relations.note: Hercules alters or displaces violent practices attributed to Saturnian Italy.
Late inconsistent Roman accounts describe a disguised Italian Faunus testing Hercules.
Both are mortal-born benefactors elevated to godhood and later shared a temple.
Hercules discovers the stolen cattle and kills Cacus.

relations.myth: Battle with the fire-breathing cave monster
relations.note: Hercules tears open Cacus’ cave and strangles Vulcan’s monstrous son.
In a rationalized variant, Hercules defeats the barbarian chieftain Cacus in war.
Hercules subdues Cerberus, brings him alive above ground, then returns him.
Hercules kills Nessus with a poisoned arrow after the centaur attacks Deianira.
Nessus’ poisoned blood later causes Hercules’ fatal burning and pyre.
Hercules defeats Antaeus by lifting him away from his sustaining mother Earth.
Hercules kills Geryon and drives his cattle through Italy.
A poorly attested tradition makes Caca betray her brother to Hercules.

relations.myth: Marriage after the contest with Achelous
relations.note: Hercules wins Deianira after defeating her river-god suitor Achelous.
Roman Hercules naturalizes the Greek Heracles’ genealogy, Labours, death, and apotheosis.
Etruscan Hercle was closely equated with Roman Hercules despite distinctive local mythology.
Greek and Roman writers identify the Tyrian and Gaditan Melqart as Heracles or Hercules.
